technical.lead: The EU AI Act's transparency article starts applying and enforcement begins
technical.body: Article 50 of the EU AI Act starts applying today, and the European Commission marked the date by confirming that its AI Office and national authorities are now enforcing it. Four situations are covered: an AI system that interacts directly with a person has to say it is an AI; synthetic image, audio, video and text has to carry machine-readable marks so it can be detected; deployers of emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation systems have to tell the people exposed to them; and deepfakes and AI-generated text published on matters of public interest have to be labelled. Enforcement sits with national market surveillance authorities, the AI Office and the European Data Protection Supervisor, with fines reaching €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover for companies and €750,000 for EU institutions, bodies and agencies, and proportionality for small and medium enterprises written into the framework. None of the scaffolding went up on the date itself: the Commission adopted its Article 50 guidelines on Monday, July 20, and the accompanying Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content — the voluntary route to demonstrating compliance, which carries a free EU icon set for labelling — has now passed 180 signatories, with a first list published. The AI Act itself entered into force on August 1, 2024, so the distance between the law existing and this particular article biting is two years and a day.

technical.lead: California's AI Transparency Act becomes operative on August 2 by design
technical.body: California's AI Transparency Act became operative today as well, and the alignment was engineered rather than coincidental: SB 942 as passed said the chapter would become operative on January 1, 2026, and AB 853 rewrote that clause to read August 2, 2026 — the same date Article 50 of the EU AI Act starts applying. The law binds any provider of a generative AI system with more than one million monthly visitors or users that is publicly accessible in California. Those providers must embed a latent disclosure in the images, video and audio their system produces — the provider's name, the system's name and version, the time and date the content was created or altered, and a unique identifier — offer users an optional visible label, and publish a free detection tool that supports an application programming interface a user can invoke without visiting the provider's website, which accepts a URL, returns whatever provenance data it finds, and does not retain submitted content longer than it needs to. A provider that licenses its system out has to require the same latent-disclosure capability by contract and revoke the licence within 96 hours of discovering the licensee stripped it. The penalty is $5,000 per violation with each day of non-compliance counted separately, and the California Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel can each bring the action, with fees and costs to a prevailing plaintiff. Two further tranches are already dated: generative AI hosting platforms and large online platforms on January 1, 2027, and capture device manufacturers on January 1, 2028. The practical consequence of the date matching is that anyone shipping generative output into both jurisdictions now has two disclosure regimes running from the same morning — one asking for machine-readable marking, the other for a named-provider latent disclosure plus a free public detection tool.

technical.lead: Unsloth ships 2026.8.1 with DeepSeek-V4 0731 support and repins its installers
technical.body: Unsloth published version 2026.8.1 to PyPI today, its first new version since 2026.7.6 on Wednesday, July 29. It stays Apache-2.0 and still supports Python 3.9 up to but not including 3.15. The changelog frames the release as a continuation of the 2026.7.6 Kimi K3 release and lists three things: support for DeepSeek-V4 0731, a batch of Windows fixes, and general bug fixes across models and systems. A merge later the same day raised the pin in both `install.sh` and `install.ps1` to `unsloth>=2026.8.1` and `unsloth-zoo>=2026.8.1` across all five install paths, so a fresh install now resolves to the new packages rather than the July ones — the release and the thing that makes the release reachable landed on the same day, which is not how a version bump usually goes. Two of the day's other merges were escaping fixes on the path where caller-supplied strings meet the template engine. One escapes template text spliced into Jinja string literals, where an apostrophe in something like "user's question" would close the literal early and raise a template syntax error, and where an unescaped backslash was silently decoded — `\boxed{}` became a backspace followed by `oxed{}`, and a Windows path like `C:\Users\me` broke outright; the second promotes that escape helper to module level, extends it to double quotes, and applies it to the system message substituted into the predefined chat templates, taking successful renderings from 76 of 180 to 180 of 180 across fifteen predefined templates and twelve test messages.

technical.lead: Karpathy says the field is starting to leave the pelican prompt behind
technical.body: The most-discussed item of the day was a test rather than a release. Andrej Karpathy handed Claude Opus 5 the opening paragraph of The Lord of the Rings, a budget of one million tokens costing roughly $10, and a request for a three.js rendering. The model worked for about two hours and produced roughly 5,500 lines of code that procedurally rendered the passage, placing and animating polygon assets in three-dimensional coordinates. Karpathy called the result janky but fun, and said the field is starting to leave the territory where you would test a model by asking it for an SVG of a pelican on a bicycle. The shape of the test is the point, not the artefact: one prompt, a large budget, a long unattended run, and a judgement on whether what comes back holds together is a different measurement from scoring a single completion, and it is a measurement that only recently became cheap enough — roughly $10 a go — to run casually.

technical.lead: Kimi K3 costs less per token on MI355X, the only box shown using a draft model
technical.body: A benchmark posted Friday, July 31 and picked up over the weekend put Kimi K3, at 2.8 trillion parameters, on three configurations and came back with a split verdict for AMD. On eight AMD MI355X running SGLang with ROCm fixes and speculative decoding from RadixArk's Kimi-K3-DSpark draft model, a 1,024-token input and 400-token output workload decoded at 118 tokens per second single-stream and peaked at 952 tokens per second aggregate, or 119 per GPU. Eight NVIDIA B300 beat that outright at 172 single-stream, 1,568 aggregate and 196 per GPU, and a two-node, sixteen-GPU B200 configuration came last at 90 single-stream and 498 aggregate, 31 per GPU. The ordering inverts on cost: at $2.50 per GPU-hour the MI355X box returns about 48 tokens per second per dollar-hour, against about 33 for the B300 at $6.00 per GPU-hour and about 7 for the two-node B200 at $4.25 per GPU-hour. The reason the author gives is capacity rather than compute — enough HBM on the AMD box to hold a model this size without spanning nodes, which is what drags the two-node B200 configuration down to 31 tokens per second per GPU. One asymmetry sits under all of it, though: the speculative decoding credited with about 2.2 times the single-stream rate on the MI355X box has no counterpart described for either NVIDIA configuration, both of which the benchmark lists as running CUDA, so the cost ordering is not a hardware-only result. It is also one author's harness on one workload shape, resting on the three per-GPU-hour rates that author assumes.

citations.label: Wafer - Running Kimi K3 on MI355X at better performance per dollar than B300
